paragraphs: AAD-1 tackles a failure in fast image-to-video generation: a model can produce videos that barely move. The paper connects this motion collapse to unstable adversarial distillation, where a generator learns with feedback from a discriminator. Its goal is to retain one-step autoregressive generation while improving the quality of motion across the resulting sequence.

The main architectural change gives the two networks different access to context. The generator remains causal, preserving its ability to generate sequentially. The discriminator can examine the entire video in both temporal directions and assign one overall realism score. This wider view helps it detect failures that unfold over time, including long-range drift and collapsed motion.

Training also proceeds in phases. Distribution matching first brings the student closer to the teacher and establishes a stable one-step generator; adversarial distillation follows afterward. Experiments on VBench report state-of-the-art results for one-step autoregressive video generation. The findings support combining sequence-wide feedback with a carefully prepared starting point for adversarial training.
icml-2026-aad-1-asymmetric-adversarial-d.tldr: AAD-1 improves one-step autoregressive video generation through a full-sequence discriminator and a distribution-matching warm-up.

paragraphs: Shapley values and related semi-values assign credit to participants based on a utility function. Computing them exactly generally requires exponentially many utility evaluations as the number of participants grows. This paper studies how accurately they can be approximated when available memory grows only linearly with that number.

The authors develop a framework based on a vector concentration inequality, which controls estimation error across the attribution vector. For commonly used semi-values, their linear-space algorithm needs O(n/ε² log(1/δ)) utility queries to keep the probability of vector error at least ε below δ. The framework connects several existing unbiased estimators and characterizes when paired sampling helps.

The approach also allows mean squared error to be explicitly minimized for a particular utility function. This leads to Adalina, an adaptive randomized algorithm with linear time and space requirements and a theoretical improvement in mean squared error. Experiments validate the theoretical findings. The contribution therefore combines a shared analysis of existing methods with an adaptive way to improve estimation accuracy.
icml-2026-adalina-adaptive-linear-approx.tldr: Adalina adaptively improves semi-value estimation error while using linear time and memory.

paragraphs: Learning a policy from recorded demonstrations can be misleading when the demonstrator and learner have different sensory capabilities. In pixel-based tasks, the demonstrator may act on information the learner cannot observe. This creates hidden confounding: apparent relationships in the demonstrations can reflect information missing from the learner's inputs.

The paper addresses this problem for expressive policies built with flow matching. It introduces a causal offline reinforcement learning objective that optimizes worst-case policy performance under possible confounding biases. A practical implementation learns from the confounded demonstrations and uses a deep discriminator to assess how the target policy differs from the nominal behavior policy.

Across 25 pixel-based tasks, the proposed augmentation achieves a success rate 120% of that obtained by state-of-the-art methods that do not account for confounding. This means a rate 1.2 times as high, rather than a 120% increase. The findings support accounting explicitly for sensory mismatch when learning complex action distributions from offline demonstrations.
icml-2026-causal-flow-q-learning-for-rob.tldr: A causal worst-case objective improves flow-matching policies learned from demonstrations with hidden sensory confounding.

paragraphs: This paper studies a mathematical model of language generation in which an algorithm receives example strings from an unknown language and must eventually generate valid strings it has not seen. An adversary controls the presentation of examples and, in the noisy version, can insert strings outside the target language. The question is how those extra strings change what generation is possible.

For both uniform and non-uniform generation, the authors prove that allowing even one noisy string strictly reduces the collections of languages that can be generated. They also prove that tolerating one noisy string is equivalent, in these two settings, to tolerating any finite amount of noise. The first corruption therefore changes feasibility, while further finite corruption does not create additional levels of difficulty in this characterization.

That equivalence contrasts with a previously established strict noise hierarchy for generation in the limit. Using their results, the authors also characterize non-uniform noise-dependent generatability. These are statements about formal generation guarantees, clarifying how different definitions of generation respond to corrupted evidence.
icml-2026-characterizing-the-effect-of-n.tldr: For uniform and non-uniform formal language generation, one noisy example reduces feasibility as much as any finite amount of noise.

paragraphs: Diffusion generation is commonly approached as numerical integration, with the model supplying estimates along a sampling trajectory. DiFA emphasizes that these estimates also contain statistical uncertainty. It treats successive predictions of the clean signal as correlated observations whose reliability changes during generation, making earlier predictions useful evidence for later ones.

The method refines predictions through sequential state estimation without additional training. Inspired by Kalman estimation, it builds agreement across historical clean-signal predictions while accounting for the logarithmic signal-to-noise ratio. This connects the refinement process to the statistical structure of forward diffusion rather than treating every prediction as an independent, equally reliable estimate.

Combining predictions can wash out detail, so DiFA adds adaptive deviation guidance to preserve residual information. On CIFAR-10 and ImageNet, the authors report significant improvements across the evaluated FID, IS, and FD-DINOv2 metrics. The results support using uncertainty-aware prediction history to improve generative fidelity, with detail preservation playing an explicit role in the design.
icml-2026-difa-inference-time-forward-pr.tldr: DiFA improves diffusion sampling without retraining by combining uncertain historical predictions while adaptively preserving detail.

paragraphs: Private stochastic optimization commonly clips individual gradients and adds noise to protect sensitive training information. The paper identifies a consequence for optimization: these operations can leave a persistent gap between the learned solution and a stationary point. DP-C4 is designed to make the errors responsible for this solution bias shrink over time.

Its central mechanism combines coupled clipping with a shifting threshold strategy. The analysis shows that both clipping bias and noise variance vanish asymptotically. Extended sensitivity analysis and a tailored allocation of the privacy budget provide the privacy guarantee. At the same privacy level, the framework injects substantially less noise than DP-SGD.

The convergence claims distinguish problem types. For strongly convex objectives, DP-C4 converges to the optimum; for non-convex objectives, it reaches a shrinking neighborhood of a first-order stationary point. This does not amount to a global-optimum guarantee for non-convex learning. Experiments across tasks and datasets report a better privacy-utility trade-off than existing baselines, supporting the practical value of reducing persistent optimization bias.
icml-2026-eliminating-solution-bias-in-d.tldr: DP-C4 makes clipping bias and noise variance vanish asymptotically while preserving differential privacy and improving optimization guarantees.

paragraphs: ETS explores whether the benefits targeted by reinforcement learning alignment can be obtained during generation without running an additional training process. Its starting point is a formulation of masked language modeling transitions that combines a reference policy with an energy term. That term provides the adjustment needed to target the optimal reinforcement learning policy.

Because the energy term must be estimated, ETS uses online Monte Carlo computation and establishes a convergence rate for the estimate. The method therefore moves work into inference: generation is guided by an estimated quantity rather than by newly trained model parameters. The theoretical convergence result supports this estimation-based route to the target policy.

To make that computation more practical, the authors combine acceleration frameworks with tailored importance sampling estimators. They report substantially lower inference latency while proving preservation of sampling quality. Experiments cover autoregressive and diffusion language models on reasoning, coding, and science benchmarks, with consistent improvements in generation quality. The findings support inference-time computation as a useful route to alignment without post-training.
icml-2026-ets-energy-guided-test-time-sc.tldr: ETS uses inference-time energy estimation to target an optimal reinforcement learning policy without additional training.

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether the generation process of a discrete diffusion language model can reveal which model produced a response. Attribution may need to distinguish different models or closely related checkpoints and backups. The authors focus on extracting useful information from the decoding trajectory and converting it into an attribution score.

They find that confidence at each decoding step is ineffective for this purpose. Bidirectional interactions let decoded tokens influence one another, producing redundant confidence signals that hide the structure of decoding order and dependencies. Their Directed Decoding Map instead captures relationships between decoding steps, exposing structural patterns associated with particular models.

Gaussian-Trajectory Attribution then models each position in this map with a separate Gaussian distribution for each source model. Differences in trajectory log-likelihood provide the attribution score. Experiments across models, datasets, and access assumptions support the approach's effectiveness. The contribution shows how the path taken to generate a response can carry attribution evidence beyond simple per-step confidence.
icml-2026-every-step-counts-decoding-tra.tldr: Structural patterns in diffusion language models' decoding trajectories enable source attribution through Gaussian likelihood comparisons.

paragraphs: Video models can imagine future observations for a robot, but visually convincing predictions do not automatically provide useful control instructions. The paper identifies a mismatch between perceptual realism and the action-related causes of state changes. Passing predicted frames into a policy or directly decoding videos into actions can consequently produce indirect, unstable control.

MoLA introduces an intermediate representation focused on actions. Multiple pretrained inverse dynamics models examine transitions in the imagined video and infer the latent actions those transitions imply. These models use complementary semantic, depth, and flow cues. Their outputs form a mixture that connects the predicted visual changes to information useful for executing a policy.

This design gives imagined futures a structured interface to robot control, rather than requiring the policy to recover all relevant action information from predicted images. Evaluations on LIBERO, CALVIN, LIBERO-Plus, and real-world manipulation tasks report consistent gains in task success, temporal consistency, and generalization. The results support translating video predictions into action-oriented representations before using them for execution.
icml-2026-from-imagined-futures-to-execu.tldr: MoLA converts imagined robot videos into complementary latent action representations that improve manipulation performance.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning a language model for a specialized domain involves repeated decisions about data, training settings, and model failures. FT-Dojo turns that workflow into an interactive task for autonomous agents. Its benchmark contains 13 tasks across five domains and evaluates the process of adaptation, including how an agent responds to feedback.

The environment standardizes the task interface, raw-data repository, sandboxed execution, feedback protocol, and held-out evaluation. The accompanying FT-Agent uses structured plans, early validation of potential failures, and analysis of feedback at multiple levels. It iteratively revises both data choices and training strategies within this common environment.

FT-Agent achieves the best performance on 10 of the 13 tasks in the reported experiments. Controlled comparisons and repeated-run statistics provide additional support for the findings. Case studies show recovery through cumulative learning, while also exposing weaknesses in causal diagnosis and long-term planning. The benchmark therefore supplies both an initial strong baseline and a way to examine where autonomous fine-tuning still breaks down.
icml-2026-ft-dojo-towards-autonomous-llm.tldr: FT-Dojo benchmarks autonomous fine-tuning workflows, and FT-Agent leads on 10 of its 13 tasks while revealing planning and diagnosis limits.

paragraphs: Automated detection of coronary artery narrowing is constrained by a shortage of high-quality angiography data. This paper studies synthetic image editing as a way to enrich training examples. The challenge is to introduce localized stenosis while maintaining precise control over the image geometry and preserving surrounding structure.

The authors argue that diffusion editing based on soft guidance during a noise-initialized reverse process offers limited pixel-level control. Their OT-Bridge Editor instead formulates localized editing as a constrained entropic optimal transport problem. Geometric information guides the generation path, making structural control part of the editing formulation rather than relying only on soft guidance.

The evaluation examines whether the generated angiograms help downstream stenosis detection. The authors report relative gains of 27.8% on ARCADE and 23.0% on their multi-center dataset, together with consistent qualitative results. These findings support the usefulness of the synthetic images as training augmentation in the evaluated settings. The reported benefit concerns downstream detection, linking geometric editing control to a practical learning outcome.
icml-2026-geometrically-constrained-sten.tldr: OT-Bridge Editor uses geometric constraints and entropic optimal transport to synthesize angiograms that improve stenosis detection.

paragraphs: A single image directly shows only the surfaces visible to its camera. LaRI addresses the harder task of predicting geometry hidden behind those surfaces. Instead of estimating one depth per viewing ray, it predicts layered point maps representing multiple surfaces that the ray intersects.

The method is fully supervised and produces its scene reconstruction in one feed-forward pass. This gives it a direct, view-aligned representation without the iterative refinement used by some existing approaches. LaRI also predicts a ray stopping index, which determines which pixels and layers correspond to valid intersections. That additional output helps identify how much of the layered prediction should be treated as actual geometry.

To support training and evaluation, the authors construct a rendering-based annotation pipeline and annotate five public datasets. These include synthetic and real-world data covering both objects and scenes. Evaluations validate the method at both scales. The contribution combines an efficient prediction method with supervision and evaluation resources for recovering occluded geometry from one image.
icml-2026-lari-layered-ray-intersections.tldr: LaRI predicts multiple surface intersections along camera rays to reconstruct visible and occluded geometry from a single image.

paragraphs: Long clinical videos require a model to find the moments that support a prediction. Passive frame sampling or loosely grounded inspection can leave that evidence insufficiently examined. MedScope addresses this by making video understanding an iterative process of locating relevant observations, reasoning about them, and checking the resulting interpretation.

The model uses tools to search from coarse temporal regions toward finer evidence. Intermediate reasoning is interleaved with targeted retrieval and verification of the observations returned. The authors also build ClinVideoSuite to provide detailed, evidence-focused supervision. Their GA-GRPO training method rewards grounded tool use and weights learning advantages according to evidence.

MedScope reports state-of-the-art performance on full-video and fine-grained understanding benchmarks, including both in-domain and out-of-domain evaluations. The stated improvement combines stronger predictions with explicit links to localized visual evidence. This matters because the model's inspection process becomes part of how it reaches and supports an answer, rather than leaving evidence selection as a passive preprocessing step.
icml-2026-medscope-incentivizing-think-w.tldr: MedScope learns to retrieve and verify targeted clinical video evidence, improving grounded video understanding.

paragraphs: Taking larger steps along a diffusion model's deterministic sampling trajectory can make generation more efficient. The paper identifies a tension: aggressive steps and highly expressive denoisers can undermine mathematical stability certificates based on contraction, which describe suppression of errors. The authors call this tension the contractivity trap.

SteinDiff adds a correction at each inference step to regularize large solver updates. The correction accounts for local data geometry, uses a closed-form coefficient derived through Stein methods, and requires neither retraining nor reference samples. Its purpose is to adapt the update itself so that large-step sampling is less vulnerable to severe errors.

The theoretical analysis includes a score-controlled perturbation bound under distribution shifts and a Stein-based interpretation of EDM-style parameterizations. Experiments report fewer severe artifacts and improved generative quality across large-step inference settings. Together, these contributions support step-wise stabilization as a way to mitigate the practical consequences of the identified tension, without claiming that every large-step trajectory becomes stable.
icml-2026-mitigating-the-contractivity-t.tldr: SteinDiff applies reference-free, geometry-aware corrections to improve diffusion generation with large sampling steps.

paragraphs: A multimodal language model receiving a continuing stream of corrections must update efficiently without disrupting unrelated behavior. The paper identifies two obstacles. Strong visual activations can dominate the statistics used to shape edits, creating conflict between modalities, while successive edits can interfere with one another over long sequences.

M-ORE addresses these problems through separate update statistics for the text stack and visual projector. It performs continual changes within a fixed, orthogonal, low-rank edit subspace. A unified proximal-projection formulation yields a closed-form update, and a Sherman-Morrison recursion keeps the overhead of each edit constant as corrections accumulate.

Separating the statistics targets visually dominated update shaping, while the structured edit space aims to reduce interference across corrections. Experiments on multiple multimodal backbones and online editing benchmarks report consistent improvements in reliability, generality, and locality over strong baselines. The results also show favorable quality-efficiency scaling, supporting the method's suitability for repeated adaptation under tight computational and memory budgets.
icml-2026-modality-decoupled-online-recu.tldr: M-ORE separates modality-specific editing statistics and uses recursive low-rank updates to improve continual multimodal model correction.

paragraphs: Activations stored during large-batch language model training can dominate memory use. Compressing them helps only if the resulting training signal remains useful. This paper connects fast convergence to the quality of subspace projection, arguing that effective compression should reconstruct activations without systematic bias and with low variance.

PRAC divides an activation into two parts. Singular value decomposition captures a principal subspace containing dominant information. A random subspace drawn from the orthogonal complement approximates the remaining tail. This combines deliberate preservation of strong components with a sampled representation of information outside those components.

A carefully chosen scaling factor gives PRAC an unbiased gradient estimator, with minimum variance under the conditions established in the analysis. That qualification matters: the minimum-variance claim is conditional. Experiments on pre-training and fine-tuning report up to 36% lower total memory use, negligible performance degradation, and minimal computational cost. The findings support preserving activation structure while sampling the residual as an effective memory-saving strategy.
icml-2026-prac-principal-random-subspace.tldr: PRAC combines principal and random activation subspaces to reduce training memory while preserving an unbiased gradient estimate.

paragraphs: When optimizing several competing objectives, a useful outcome is a collection of designs expressing different optimal trade-offs. Batch selection must therefore consider both the quality of individual candidates and how widely they cover the Pareto set. Choosing several strong but similar candidates can leave other desirable designs unexplored.

Probability of Matching evaluates these two requirements together. It considers the likelihood that every candidate in a batch is Pareto optimal and the probability that the batch collectively covers the full Pareto set. To estimate coverage and encourage diversity, the method incorporates principles of sampling without replacement. This makes collective coverage an explicit part of selecting the next batch.

Experiments on synthetic benchmarks and real-world tasks report consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, with comparable computational efficiency. Evaluation includes standard multi-objective optimization measures and Expected Minimum Distance, a new measure of coverage in design space. The findings support judging batches by how well their candidates complement one another as well as by their individual quality.
icml-2026-probability-of-matching-for-ba.tldr: Probability of Matching selects optimization batches by jointly assessing Pareto quality and collective design-space coverage.

paragraphs: Surface reconstruction through differentiable rendering depends on connecting image appearance to geometry. Photometric ambiguity makes that connection underdetermined: matching appearance can leave the underlying surface insufficiently constrained. AmbiSuR investigates this problem within Gaussian Splatting, focusing on ambiguities built into its representation.

The authors identify two ambiguities at the level of individual primitives and find that Gaussian Splatting also contains information that can indicate ambiguity. Their framework first introduces photometric disambiguation to constrain ill-posed geometric solutions and support definite surface formation. It then uses an ambiguity indication module to identify reconstructions that remain underconstrained and guide their correction.

These components address both the formation of ambiguous geometry and the detection of unresolved regions. Experiments report better surface reconstruction than existing methods across challenging scenarios, alongside broad compatibility. The stated findings suggest that the representation can contribute to diagnosing its own reconstruction uncertainty, making ambiguity analysis useful for both preventing geometric errors and directing subsequent corrections.
icml-2026-revisiting-photometric-ambigui.tldr: AmbiSuR improves Gaussian-Splatting surface reconstruction by constraining photometric ambiguities and identifying underconstrained geometry.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards can improve language model reasoning while concentrating generation on a narrow range of solutions. SetPO addresses this loss of diversity by evaluating sampled reasoning trajectories as a set. Its objective reflects diminishing returns: another trajectory should contribute less when it resembles those already present.

The method measures similarity through a kernel and computes each trajectory's contribution by comparing the set with and without that trajectory. This leave-one-out contribution becomes a plug-in term that shapes the advantage used in policy optimization. Diversity thus affects the learning signal alongside the rewards already driving reasoning performance.

A distribution-perturbation analysis proves a monotonicity property within the proposed framework: rarer trajectories make larger marginal contributions to global diversity. Across model scales and reasoning benchmarks, experiments report improvements over strong baselines in both Pass@1 and Pass@K. These findings support encouraging varied trajectories while improving success with both a single attempt and multiple sampled attempts.
icml-2026-setpo-set-level-policy-optimiz.tldr: SetPO rewards each reasoning trajectory's contribution to set diversity, improving both single-attempt and multiple-attempt success.

paragraphs: A model's response to an isolated prompt may not reveal how safely it behaves after an extended conversation. This paper examines safety through the evolution of conversational state. It argues that many multi-turn failures arise from changing context, which prompt-level analysis alone does not fully capture.

STAR is a diagnostic framework that treats dialogue history as an operator changing the model's state. It enables controlled study of safety behavior along interaction trajectories. The purpose is to probe how an aligned model crosses a safety boundary under autoregressive conditioning, rather than to optimize the strength of an attack.

Across multiple frontier models, systems that appear robust in static evaluations show rapid, reproducible safety collapse during structured multi-turn interactions. Mechanistic analysis finds monotonic movement away from refusal-related representations and abrupt transitions induced by role-conditioned context. These findings support evaluating safety as a property of evolving conversations. They establish a failure pattern in the studied settings, rather than implying that every extended conversation causes collapse.
icml-2026-state-dependent-safety-failure.tldr: STAR shows how evolving conversational context can produce reproducible safety failures in models that appear robust on isolated prompts.

paragraphs: GPU application performance depends on both efficient kernels and the host-side settings that coordinate them. StitchCUDA addresses end-to-end program generation, extending beyond optimization of isolated kernels. Its framework divides responsibility among a Planner for system design, a Coder for implementation, and a Verifier for correctness checks and performance profiling.

The Coder receives reinforcement learning on two skills: translating tasks into code and improving code from feedback. Training combines rubric-based rewards with rule-based rewards from real executions. This supports advanced CUDA techniques such as custom kernel fusion and cuBLAS epilogues while discouraging benchmark shortcuts such as copying PyTorch implementations or hardcoding outputs.

On KernelBench, StitchCUDA reports nearly 100% success on end-to-end programming tasks. Its reported speedup is 1.72 times that of the multi-agent baseline and 2.73 times that of the reinforcement-learning model baselines. The findings support combining specialized agent roles with execution-grounded coder training to improve complete GPU programs, where performance depends on interactions across the system.
icml-2026-stitchcuda-an-automated-multi-.tldr: StitchCUDA combines specialized agents and execution-grounded reinforcement learning to generate and optimize complete GPU programs.

paragraphs: Limited training data, translation noise, and unstable alignment across languages make adaptation difficult for low-resource languages. LiRA addresses these problems by fine-tuning existing pretrained models with a framework designed to keep representations and downstream behavior consistent across languages. It combines shared semantic alignment with a language-aware output component.

The first component, Arca, aligns low-resource inputs with an English semantic space through anchors and collaborative encoding. The second, LaSR, promotes cross-lingual consistency for retrieval, ranking, and reasoning. The theoretical result is conditional: bounded anchoring error and translation-induced bias yield bounded representation deviation, with stable downstream behavior under local Lipschitz continuity.

The authors also introduce a multilingual product retrieval dataset spanning five Southeast Asian and two South Asian languages. Experiments on retrieval, ranking, question answering, and reasoning report consistent improvements over strong multilingual and language-model baselines. Together, the analysis and experiments support anchored adaptation, while keeping the mathematical stability claim tied to its stated error and continuity assumptions.
icml-2026-toward-robust-multilingual-ada.tldr: LiRA improves low-resource multilingual adaptation through English semantic anchors and language-aware consistency, with conditional stability guarantees.

paragraphs: Sharing one policy across agents can improve learning efficiency, but agents with different capabilities may need different behaviors. Giving each agent an independent policy avoids some conflicts while weakening knowledge transfer. Dspic seeks to retain the benefits of sharing while accommodating heterogeneous roles and multiple possible patterns of coordinated action.

The method uses self-supervised learning to extract discriminative role embeddings. These embeddings guide a complete division of the observation space, for which the paper provides a theoretical guarantee concerning the optimality of parameter sharing. A diffusion policy then handles the more complex and varied action distributions associated with that division, within a maximum entropy framework.

The design combines role differentiation with a shared learning mechanism instead of requiring separate policies for every agent. Experiments on MaMuJoCo, SMAC, SMACv2, and LBF report superior sample efficiency while maintaining asymptotic optimality. The findings support using learned roles and expressive action modeling to address the tension between specialization and knowledge transfer in multi-agent learning.
icml-2026-towards-complete-multi-agent-c.tldr: Dspic combines learned agent roles with a shared diffusion policy to improve efficient coordination across heterogeneous agents.

paragraphs: Complex CAD modeling connects a sequence of parametric operations with the geometric boundaries those operations produce. Operations such as fillets and chamfers require selecting particular boundary primitives. The paper identifies a gap in methods that treat parametric program generation and direct boundary representation synthesis as separate problems.

FutureCAD connects these capabilities through executable CadQuery scripts and a transformer called BRepGround. The language model describes geometric selections using natural-language queries. BRepGround maps those descriptions to the intended boundary primitives, allowing generated programs to refer to geometry needed by advanced modeling operations.

The authors construct a training dataset of real-world CAD models. Supervised fine-tuning develops the language model's initial generation abilities, followed by reinforcement learning intended to improve generalization. Experiments report state-of-the-art CAD generation performance. The central contribution is an interface between program instructions and explicit geometric selection, enabling the generated modeling process to use the boundary structure created by earlier operations.
icml-2026-towards-high-fidelity-cad-gene.tldr: FutureCAD links generated CAD programs to boundary geometry by grounding natural-language selections in specific geometric primitives.

paragraphs: Tool-using agents face safety risks that unfold across several interactions and tool operations. This paper develops a taxonomy for turning single-turn harmful tasks into multi-turn attack sequences. The resulting MT-AgentRisk benchmark evaluates safety in settings that combine extended interaction with realistic tool use.

Experiments across open and closed models report an average 16% increase in attack success rate in multi-turn settings. This finding indicates that evaluating harmful requests only in isolation can miss vulnerabilities introduced by a longer interaction. The benchmark provides a systematic way to construct and examine those extended sequences.

The proposed defense, ToolShield, learns safety experience through self-exploration without training and without depending on a specific tool. When encountering a new tool, the agent generates test cases, executes them, observes downstream effects, and distills the results for deployment. Experiments report an average 30% reduction in attack success rate during multi-turn interactions. The findings support proactive exploration of tool behavior as a defense against the measured risks.
icml-2026-unsafer-in-many-turns-benchmar.tldr: MT-AgentRisk exposes increased safety failures across multiple turns, while ToolShield reduces attacks through training-free exploration of tool behavior.
